# Verification, Feedback, and Learning {#sec-feedback-verification-trust}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!"*
>
> — Edsger W. Dijkstra, *Notes on Structured Programming* (1970) [@Dijkstra1970Notes]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's note.** Dijkstra's warning separates a check from the stronger claim
someone might attach to it. Passing tests supports only the conditions and
behaviors the tests exercised. A failed test can still decisively contradict a
bounded claim.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
What signal came back from AI-assisted design work, what does it say about a
named action, artifact, assumption, or result, and what should the project
learn or change because of it?
:::

Architecture work receives returned signals from tools and environments,
human reviewers, learned methods, and deployed systems or silicon.
Verification is the claim-specific work that determines whether a return is
trustworthy and what, if anything, it can support. Empirical checks qualify
observed or computed quantities from runs, experiments, prototypes, or deployed
systems. Dynamic verification is one empirical form in which tests, simulation,
or emulation exercise an artifact and observe named behaviors. Formal methods
instead use mathematical models and logic to establish the status of a property
over a model under stated assumptions [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. These
approaches are complementary, not interchangeable. Feedback
interprets the qualified result for the named object and identifies the next
justified action. Learning is what the work improves or retains because of that
interpretation. A return may report a measurement, expose a failure, localize a
cause, challenge a rationale, or leave a question unresolved. A recorded update
is justified only when the record names what produced the return, what it refers
to, when it was obtained, and what kind of update it supports.

Architecture studies combine empirical measurements, formal results,
simulation, physical analysis, model predictions, reviews, and field
observations. These signals do not share one meaning of *pass*, one type of
uncertainty, or one scope. The chapter problem is to qualify each return for
the property it can address, compare like with like, expose what remains
unchecked, and route the result without letting the signal decide its own use.

The constructed Lighthouse cache fixture later in the chapter gives these
distinctions one concrete case. It records illustrative chronology and missing
fields rather than claiming an executed cache study. A returned number is not
automatically a measurement. A measurement is not automatically a valid
comparison. A valid comparison supports only the property, candidate,
conditions, and check scope that produced it.

The AI-assisted methods considered here may produce and score candidates faster,
search directly against imperfect proxies, and generate explanations that sound
more certain than the measurements allow. That acceleration does not remove the
property-specific verification obligation. Each candidate still needs a check
with a declared property, an adequate reference or expected-result rule,
recorded conditions, and coverage. Generated tests or properties create their
own adequacy questions. Candidate production can scale while the work needed
to qualify a result remains the bottleneck. AI does not change what an
architecture result must contain.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Qualify returned fields as measurements, formal results, diagnostics, or
  unresolved signals while preserving lineage and execution status.
- Build matched comparisons with named candidates, comparators, quantities,
  conditions, uncertainty, and decision margins.
- Interpret empirical uncertainty and formal status without widening the
  property, assumptions, bounds, or coverage.
- Test proxies and explanations for support, numerical calibration, confounding,
  variability, selection bias, and robustness.
- Use qualified feedback to choose the next action and decide what to retain
  within a run, across a project, and for later work without turning every
  result into training data.

:::

## From Returned Signal to Retained Learning {#sec-from-feedback-to-decision}

Execution, verification, feedback, and learning answer different questions.
The environment records whether a request was valid, what ran, what failed,
which artifacts returned, and what state and cost accompanied the attempt.
This chapter begins after that record exists. Verification asks whether a
returned field measures the requested quantity, bears on a named property,
and can support a comparison or revision. Feedback interprets the qualified
result for its target and identifies the next justified action. Learning
determines what that action should improve now and what the project should
retain.

The progression runs from a returned signal to a qualified result, from that
result to a supported claim, from the claim to a justified action, and from the
action to retained learning. A later step cannot repair a missing earlier one.

Not every source returns a measurement. A review rationale, model
critique, proof status, counterexample, or tool warning may still be useful
when its source, target, scope, timing, and limitations are recorded. A
numerical return needs additional qualification before it can support a
comparison.

A failed setup is not a poor measurement of a candidate. It is no candidate
measurement at all. A clean process exit may still return a partial report,
omit a required field, use the wrong unit, or parse an unfamiliar warning as
success. A complete return can contain a genuine limit violation. Execution
status must survive intact so interpretation can distinguish these cases.

An incomplete attempt does not make every returned artifact unusable, but any
salvage is claim-specific. An individual field or artifact may proceed to
qualification only when the declared run specification and expected outputs
treat it as independently complete, its extraction and lineage are valid,
termination could not have changed its meaning or observation window, and the
claim does not depend on missing state. Otherwise, quarantine it with the
attempt.
Salvaging one field does not relabel the overall timed-out or incomplete
attempt as complete. Every other claim remains unresolved.

The reader must therefore keep five questions separate. Did the requested work
execute? Is the returned artifact structurally and semantically valid for its
intended downstream use? Is the measurement or formal result valid under its
stated conditions? Which requirement or check does it satisfy or contradict,
and what remains uncovered? What architecture conclusion or revision, if any,
does it support? A yes to any one question never answers those that follow.

Consider a generated RTL block. Its invocation may complete and return RTL,
logs, and a timing report. The RTL may parse yet fail elaboration or library
binding, or it may fail a downstream interface or semantic check. The artifact
is then invalid for its intended tool path. For an artifact that does elaborate,
a timing report may still leave endpoints unconstrained or use the wrong mode
or corner, which makes that result invalid for the timing claim. Even a
qualified timing result supports only the named timing requirement. Power,
functional correctness, and security remain uncovered, and the timing result
alone does not select the architecture.

A returned signal gains meaning only as it passes distinct, claim-specific
qualifications (@fig-evidence-flow). Each completed step adds something the
preceding step did not establish. Verification begins by asking whether the
returned artifact is structurally and semantically fit for its intended
downstream use, then binds the valid artifact to its type, target, meaning, and
conditions. The figure keeps artifact validity inside result qualification
rather than drawing a separate box. Its middle path is conditional.
Comparative empirical claims need a matched comparator, while a proof status,
warning, review rationale, or counterexample needs a property-specific check of
its target, meaning, assumptions, and limits. An incomplete return can route
directly to execution, and an invalid check can route directly to study
formulation.

![**A tool return gains meaning through claim-specific qualification**: The
execution record first supplies a return with status and lineage. Result
qualification binds its type, target, meaning, and conditions. A comparison
supporting a comparative claim adds a matched comparator; formal and other
returns follow the property check appropriate to their type. Feedback scopes
the interpretation of what the result supports and does not support before the
project records what to improve or retain.](images/F8-evidence-flow){#fig-evidence-flow
width="88%" fig-alt="A five-step flow from tool return through verification and
a comparison or property check to feedback and a learning step that records
what to improve or retain. Side paths send incomplete returns to execution
repair and invalid checks to study formulation."}

The execution record supplies a return with status and lineage. Result
qualification within verification first establishes whether the artifact is
usable downstream, then determines its type, target, meaning, and conditions.
The next stage matches the result to the claim. A measurement supporting a
comparative claim needs a comparator, difference, and uncertainty. A formal
status needs a property, model, assumptions, and proof scope. Other return types
need an equally explicit target and check. Feedback then interprets the result
within that scope, stating what it supports, what it does not, and which next
action is justified. Learning records what the work should improve or retain. A
missing execution field routes back to the environment, while an invalid
comparison or property check routes back to study formulation. Feedback becomes
useful by identifying which object needs attention, not by prescribing its own
update. Those qualifications also depend on what produced the return, because
different signal sources expose different properties and limitations.

## Sources of Returned Signals

Human reviewers, architecture tools, learned methods, and deployed systems all
return signals. Their differences determine what later qualification must
establish rather than creating one preferred source (@tbl-feedback-sources).
No source combines complete context, immediate response, precise localization,
and decision-relevant coverage.

| **Signal source** | **Common form** | **Timing and locality** | **Main quality question** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Human reviewer | Critique, rationale, missing constraint, or priority judgment. | Intermittent and often context-rich; locality depends on the review. | Does the reviewer have the relevant context, expertise, and authority, and is the rationale recorded? |
| Architecture tool or experiment | Scalar, trace, report, counterexample, diagnostic, or proof status. | Immediate to multi-day; may identify one path or only a terminal outcome. | Which property did the tool observe, under which conditions, with what coverage and error? |
| Learned model or method | Prediction, ranking, score, critique, or explanation. | Usually fast and dense; often tied to the supplied representation. | Does the predicted score agree with stronger checks in the region being used, and which assumptions does it share with the producer? |
| Deployed system or silicon | Telemetry, characterization result, incident, or user-visible symptom. | Delayed and sparse; often system-level rather than component-local. | Which population, version, workload, and unobserved causes limit the inference? |

: **Sources of returned signals differ in form, timing, and locality**: Quality
depends on whether a signal is fit for the learning or revision it is asked to
support.
{#tbl-feedback-sources tbl-colwidths="[18,25,27,30]"}

No source dominates the others. Fast, dense signals are often narrow or
proxy-based; direct field signals may be delayed and confounded; contextual
review may be authoritative but intermittent. The architecture consequence is
to select and qualify a source for the property and action at hand rather than
treating speed, density, or direct observation as evidence quality.

A delayed signal can resolve an outcome while teaching little about how to
revise the work. A three-day place-and-route and timing run may show that a
candidate missed timing, but the final result does not identify which of
thousands of generated choices caused the miss. Revision needs a signal at the
right locality, such as path slack linked to the graph node, parameter, or
transformation that changed.

Feedback engineering offers a useful precedent. It separates whether the state
needed for a corrective action is observable from the design of that action,
and it treats delay as part of the feedback path
[@AstromMurray2008FeedbackSystems]. A multi-day architecture tool return can
leave the cause of a failure only partially observable even when the final
outcome is clear. The analogy stops there. This chapter does not model design
search as a linear controller; it borrows the narrower lesson that available
signals and their delay limit which correction is justified.

Handling that delayed result begins with lineage rather than causal
attribution. Bind the return to the exact candidate, parent actions, represented
state, constraints, tool and checker versions, seed, checkpoint, workload, and
software conditions that produced it. Lineage alone does not qualify the
return. When execution, setup, extraction, and check conditions are valid, the
terminal result can establish that this candidate missed timing under those
conditions. It does not yet establish which earlier action caused the miss.

The next step is a distinguishing comparison. Inspect path endpoints,
constraint coverage, congestion, power-density maps, and the differences from
the parent or a matched sibling. A stale constraint or broken setup routes the
revision to the environment or representation. Repeated failure across a
matched proposal class, after shared setup and conditions are checked, can
justify reopening the method or study and asking whether the representation,
shared constraints, or proposal process needs to change. A localized mechanism
supported by the comparison can justify a design revision. If no diagnostic
separates those possibilities, preserve the terminal outcome and leave the
mechanism unresolved rather than turning every upstream action into a negative
label.

Deployment feedback follows the same rule. A field result attaches first to the
shipped hardware, software, workload, and operating conditions it observed.
Those conditions may reopen an earlier claim, but the field symptom does not
identify the responsible design choice until an additional comparison or
diagnostic supports that attribution.

Dense, immediate feedback is easier for a method to learn from, but it is often
a proxy. Feedback that observes a decision-relevant property may be slower,
more expensive, or less frequent. Fast proxy signals can guide search only
inside their validated range. Slower or less frequent checks can test
properties the proxy omits. Each signal should therefore be qualified by its
latency, granularity, execution cost, uncertainty, interpretation time, and
review cost.

Empirical returns take the first qualification path. The next question is
whether a numerical value is eligible to enter the comparison the architecture
claim requires.

## Qualifying Empirical Measurements

An empirical measurement is an observed or computed quantity from a run,
experiment, implementation flow, prototype, or deployed system under recorded
conditions. It may carry sampling variation, run-to-run variability, numerical
tolerance, and model error. Those limits differ from the logical status of a
formal result.

A measurement record needs enough information to answer six questions
(@tbl-measurement-record).

| **Field** | **Question the record must answer** |
| --- | --- |
| **Candidate identity** | Which design revision, configuration, software state, and workload produced the value? |
| **Quantity and unit** | What property was measured or computed, how was it aggregated, and in what unit? |
| **Conditions** | Which tool, model, configuration, corner, seed where relevant, and operating conditions apply? |
| **Extraction status** | Did the expected artifact exist, parse under the declared schema, and retain unfamiliar warnings? |
| **Variation and error** | What repetitions, sampling method, numerical tolerance, model error, or known bound limits the value? |
| **Source record** | Which returned artifact and execution attempt support the field, and can the value be recovered from them? |

: **A measurement is a returned value with identity, meaning, conditions, and
limits**: These fields test whether the execution record is sufficient for the
comparison being attempted.
{#tbl-measurement-record tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Together, these fields form an admission test for a measurement rather than six
independent quality scores. They make the value interpretable, bound its use,
and keep it recoverable from the attempt that produced it. Passing that test
does not make a comparison valid. It makes the returned value eligible to enter
one.

For sampled workloads or repeated flows, the record also names the unit of
observation, target population, sampling window, aggregation, and dependence
structure. Missing or censored observations remain visible rather than
disappearing from the aggregate. These fields separate a quantity computed
correctly from an estimate that represents the population and decision the
study actually names.

The environment provides returned artifacts, extraction status, recorded
conditions, and lineage; measurement qualification does not reconstruct
missing versions or rerun a parser. It asks whether the quantity, aggregation,
error, comparator, and check scope make the returned field usable as a
measurement. Missing execution fields require an environment repair.
Inadequate observations or an invalid comparison require a change to the
study.

The compact Lighthouse fixture below includes the fields needed to teach
feedback qualification (@tbl-lighthouse-feedback-record). It is an
author-created teaching artifact, not a tool log or a measured cache study.
Every event and value is illustrative. The fixture supports no cache execution
fact, and it leaves the evidence that a real run would require visibly
unreported.

| **Illustrative record and chronology** | **Candidate and requested work** | **Illustrative execution status and return** | **Missing evidence and dispatch state** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SRAM-2-A1`, `SRAM-3-A1`, and `SRAM-4-A1`, before the illustrative cycle attempts | `L2-2M-A`, `L2-3M-A`, and `L2-4M-A`; one hypothetical SRAM area and access-time screen per candidate under the declared process, voltage, and temperature conditions. | The fixture indicates a return for each. Illustrative area and access-time pairs are $1.2\,\mathrm{mm}^2$ and $2.1\,\mathrm{ns}$, $1.4\,\mathrm{mm}^2$ and $2.4\,\mathrm{ns}$, and $1.7\,\mathrm{mm}^2$ and $2.8\,\mathrm{ns}$. | Exact terminal status, serialized inputs, raw and parsed artifacts, parser status, energy, leakage, and realized cost are not supplied. The fixture depicts cycle-level simulator requests for the 2\ MiB and 3\ MiB candidates and no 4\ MiB request, but it supplies no dispatch event or reason. |
| `SIM-2-A1`, illustrative cycle attempt 1 of 4 | `L2-2M-A`; one hypothetical cycle-level baseline simulation with the fixed workload and software. | The fixture indicates a baseline frame summary and an illustrative subsystem power value of $2.90\,\mathrm{W}$. It supplies no terminal status. | Matched frame records, clean-state and artifact identities, parser fields, output lineage, and realized cost are not supplied. |
| `SIM-3-A1`, illustrative cycle attempt 2 of 4 | `L2-3M-A`; one hypothetical cycle-level candidate simulation. | The fixture labels `SIM-3-A1` as a stale-constraint-state setup failure with no candidate return. | Diagnostics, partial artifacts, retry parent, reset action, output lineage, and realized cost are not supplied. |
