Its fourth illustrative attempt reaches the constructed cycle-attempt limit. | The returned values, starting and reset-state identities, raw and parsed artifacts, parser status, repeat lineage, and realized cost are not supplied. |
| `SIM-3-SUMMARY-A`, after illustrative attempts 3 and 4 | `L2-3M-A`; a hypothetical grouped frame, cache, and power summary. | The fixture indicates a derived summary without depicting another tool dispatch. | Values, per-attempt attribution, input artifact identities, derivation version, and processing cost are not supplied. |

: **The constructed Lighthouse fixture illustrates chronology but contains no
measurement evidence**: It is an author-created teaching artifact rather than
measured project data, and every event and numerical value is illustrative.
Missing artifacts and fields remain unreported. The fixture therefore
establishes no cache execution fact, candidate result, or disposition.
{#tbl-lighthouse-feedback-record tbl-colwidths="[20,20,25,35]"}

The fixture makes two distinctions inspectable. It labels `SIM-3-A1` as a setup
failure rather than a negative candidate result. Its later 3\ MiB entries indicate
returns but omit the values, artifacts, state identities, parser status, and
lineage needed to qualify them. The 4\ MiB entry depicts no simulator request and
supplies no dispatch evidence that could explain why. The fixture therefore
establishes chronology and known missingness only. It prevents an infrastructure
failure from becoming negative training data and a favorable value with unknown
conditions from becoming evidence merely because its unit looks familiar.

Once a value is qualified, it can enter the comparison that the architecture
question requires. Qualification establishes what one return means.
Comparison establishes what differs between the candidate and a declared
alternative under matched conditions.

Empirical uncertainty and formal proof status answer different questions. An
empirical interval summarizes variation under a sampling and repetition
procedure. Its interpretation depends on the population, statistic, dependence
structure, model error, and decision margin. A formal result is not a narrow
empirical interval and has no sampling confidence level. It reports a logical
outcome for a stated property, model, and assumptions. Solver time, proof
depth, and memory limit its scope or completion, not its statistical
confidence. Before the chapter resumes comparison, formal returns must pass a
parallel qualification path over the stated property, model, assumptions, and
proof scope.

## Formal Verification and Its Scope

Formal verification follows the same qualification path without becoming an
empirical measurement or necessarily requiring a matched comparator. Its
returned status begins with three objects. The *property* states the behavior
to check. The *model* defines the state, transitions, and artifacts over which
the property is interpreted. The *assumptions* restrict inputs, environment
behavior, reset, clocks, protocols, or neighboring components. A formal result
is meaningful only when all three travel with it. A proof over the wrong model
or under an impossible assumption can be logically sound and architecturally
useless.

The checked model may differ from the RTL or implementation artifact named in
the architecture claim. Elaboration, extraction, or abstraction may add or
remove behaviors. The result must state what correspondence the flow preserves
between the model and claimed artifact and why that relation lets the proved
property carry to the claimed artifact [@Clarke2018ModelChecking].

The result also depends on a trusted checking base, the steps and components
that turn the architecture artifact and requirement into the problem the solver
actually checks. The record identifies elaboration or model extraction,
property translation, relevant libraries and scripts, the solver or proof
checker, and any certificate or replay path. A proof can be logically valid for
a mistranslated property or the wrong extracted model and still fail the
architecture requirement. When a tool produces a checkable proof certificate or
replay artifact, retain it. Some tools return no such artifact, so the record
must not imply that one exists.

The returned status should distinguish four outcomes:

- **Proved:** The recorded checking path reported that the stated property or
  equivalence relation holds for the declared model and assumptions. The claim
  remains conditional on the recorded property translation, model-to-artifact
  relation, trusted checking components, and any checkable certificate or replay
  artifact the tool provides. A proof method need not be complete for a proved
  result to be valid.
- **Counterexample:** The tool returned a modeled trace that violates the
  property. The trace still needs setup and assumption review before it is
  treated as a realizable architecture failure.
- **Bounded-only:** No counterexample was found through the declared horizon.
  The result says nothing beyond that bound unless a separate completeness
  argument applies.
- **Inconclusive:** The solver returned `unknown`, exhausted time or memory,
  failed to complete induction, or otherwise supplied no proof or
  counterexample. Resource exhaustion is not partial correctness.

Bounded model checking searches modeled traces through a finite bound $k$
under stated assumptions [@BiereEtAl1999BMC]. Failing to find a counterexample
through $k$ does not exclude a longer one. An unbounded safety conclusion
requires a completeness argument or an unbounded method such as induction or
a property-directed reachability method such as IC3
[@Bradley2011IC3; @EenEtAl2011PDR]. Even then, the result covers only the
stated property over the modeled transition system and assumptions.

Safety and liveness make different claims. A safety property excludes a bad
behavior, such as two requesters simultaneously holding exclusive ownership of
one cache line. Proving such a safety property without a bound still does not
establish progress. A liveness property requires progress, such as an accepted request eventually
receiving a response [@AlpernSchneider1985Liveness;
@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. A bounded response check can expose a slow or stuck
execution within its horizon, but it does not prove that starvation or deadlock
is impossible beyond that horizon. An unbounded progress claim needs a
liveness-capable proof or a justified reduction, and it must retain the
fairness assumptions that rule out indefinitely postponed actions. Unrealistic
fairness assumptions can hide an architectural progress defect. The result
therefore records the property class, fairness assumptions, proof method, and
any bound or reduction used.

A property can pass without checking the intended behavior. *Vacuity* occurs
when a condition that should trigger the property never occurs, so the
implication is always true [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity;
@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. A nonvacuous property can still be weak. It may allow
a response thousands of cycles late, omit exclusivity, ignore reset, or check
one requester while leaving another unconstrained. Teams can exercise
properties with cover statements, reachable triggers, known positive and
negative cases, mutation, and review against the requirement they are meant to
express. Systems such as AssertLLM generate SystemVerilog assertions from
design specifications and evaluate them against golden register-transfer-level
(RTL) designs with formal property verification [@FangEtAl2025AssertLLM]. If
the RTL and assertions inherit the same missing requirement, a clean proof
still says nothing about the omitted behavior.

Equivalence checking asks whether two artifacts preserve a declared relation.
Combinational equivalence can pair state elements as cut points and compare the
combinational logic between them. Sequential equivalence is needed when
transformations such as retiming, latency changes, additional state, or a
changed reset mapping alter correspondence across state or time. Neither form
establishes that the reference artifact expresses the intended architecture
[@Kropf1999FormalVerification].

Equivalence is also too strong when an implementation intentionally adds
detail or permits fewer behaviors than an abstract specification. A refinement
check instead asks whether each implementation behavior allowed by the mapping
remains within the specification. Large proofs are often decomposed by
component. In an assume-guarantee argument, each block proves a guarantee only
while its environment satisfies named assumptions; the composition is sound
only when neighboring guarantees discharge those assumptions
[@BenvenisteEtAl2018Contracts]. A block proof does not silently become a
whole-system proof. The refinement mapping, component boundaries, assumptions,
and unproved remainder remain part of the result.

Review must also trace each architectural requirement to the property or
relation meant to cover it. The record keeps the requirement source, claimed
RTL or implementation artifact, checked model, property or relation,
assumptions, and the abstraction or extraction relation between the model and
artifact. It also identifies elaboration or model extraction, property
translation, relevant libraries and scripts, the solver or proof checker, and
any checkable proof certificate or replay artifact the tool provides. Proof
method and status, bound or completeness basis, vacuity or cover evidence,
refinement or composition boundary, and the explicitly uncovered remainder
complete the record. A clean set of proofs does not establish that the property
set is complete.

Dynamic simulation makes a different claim. Directed tests,
constrained-random stimuli, coverage-guided generation, emulation, formal
methods, and post-silicon testing complement one another because exhaustive
simulation is generally infeasible [@Kropf1999FormalVerification]. Code
coverage reports exercised structures. Functional coverage reports events or
bins defined by the verification plan. SystemVerilog defines
functional-coverage constructs such as
covergroups, coverpoints, bins, and crosses [@IEEE2023SystemVerilog]. Neither
coverage family reports the fraction of every reachable behavior checked, while
a formal proof covers no property that was never written.

Published accounts of the Pentium floating-point division (FDIV) failure
document both the missing table entries and Intel's \$475 million pretax charge
[@Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Intel1995PentiumCharge].

::: {.callout-war-story title="The Pentium FDIV bug and the limit of sampled testing"}
**The claim.** Pre-silicon testing supported the implemented floating-point
division behavior over the cases it exercised.

**The gap.** Five missing table entries escaped testing and produced incorrect
results for rare operand pairs. Intel later reported a \$475 million pretax
charge for replacement and associated costs.

**The lesson.** Sampled tests cannot support an unbounded absence claim.
Another check is needed when the property demands one.
:::

Formal verification later became the primary validation method for the
execution cluster in Intel's Core i7 flow [@KaivolaEtAl2009Corei7Formal]. With
that parallel qualification path established, the chapter returns to matched
empirical comparison, where the claim depends on a declared comparator,
conditions, and uncertainty rather than formal proof scope.

## Matching Measurements to Claims {#sec-evidence-specific-to-claim-and-scope}

This section asks whether an observed comparison supports a difference under
matched conditions.

Architecture decisions usually depend on differences rather than isolated
values. A cache study asks how a candidate differs from a baseline under the
same workload and software state. Two candidates produced by different
processes can also be compared here, but the result is limited to their
measured design difference rather than the quality of the complete workflows
that produced them. The comparator is part of the claim, not a footnote added
after the result.

A comparison must bind two designs to one measured difference and to the scope
that limits it (@fig-claim-frame).

![**A comparison binds two designs to one measured difference and its
limits**: Candidate and comparator are evaluated for the same quantity and
unit. The result remains conditional on workload and state, tool conditions,
uncertainty, and the property the check can observe.](images/F7-claim-frame){#fig-claim-frame
width="100%" fig-alt="Three-column comparison frame. Candidate
and comparator feed a measured quantity, difference, and uncertainty, which
are bounded by workload and design state, tool conditions, and check scope."}

The candidate and comparator enter as explicit revisions and configurations.
Both feed the same quantity and unit
before the center column states their difference and its uncertainty. The
right-hand column binds that result to workload and design state, tool and
operating conditions, and the check's scope and nonclaims. A different scope
creates a different comparison even when the center value is unchanged.

For matched cases $c_j$, the basic paired difference is

$$
d_j = y(\text{candidate}, c_j) - y(\text{comparator}, c_j).
$$

The sign convention must be stated. Positive may mean improvement for
throughput and regression for latency. A percentage must name its
denominator. An aggregate must state whether it is a mean, percentile, maximum,
geometric mean, or another statistic. For positive ratios normalized to a
reference, the geometric mean preserves the relative interpretation across a
benchmark set; an arithmetic mean of those ratios can depend on which system is
chosen as the reference [@FlemingWallace1986HowNotToLie]. Without those choices,
two correct numbers can still form an incoherent comparison.

### Matching Factors That Can Change the Result

The candidate and comparator should differ only along the factors the study
intends to compare. Workload, software, model version, tool flags, operating
point, warmup, sampling window, and resource budget can all create a
difference that has nothing to do with the architecture change. A matched
comparison records them rather than relying on similar filenames or a shared
directory.

Systematic model error sometimes cancels in a relative comparison. It does so
only when the model treats the candidate and comparator similarly in the
region being studied. A frozen simulator can support an ordering even when its
absolute prediction differs from silicon, but that bargain fails when the
architecture change crosses an unmodeled boundary or affects one candidate
differently. Cancellation is a hypothesis to check, not a property of using
the same tool [@GutierrezEtAl2014SourcesOfError;
@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity].

### Differences and Their Uncertainty

Repeated measurements estimate run-to-run variability when the flow or
workload is variable. Paired resampling can preserve the relationship between
matched baseline and candidate frames.[^fn-paired-block-resampling-c07] The
resampled object is the paired-difference sequence $d_j$, not two independently
resampled streams. The resulting interval assumes that this sequence is
sufficiently stationary over the sampled region and that the declared block
length preserves the dependence relevant to the statistic. Numerical
tolerances, finite sampling, heuristic variation, and model error may require
different treatments. One generic error bar cannot represent all of them.

[^fn-paired-block-resampling-c07]: **Paired block resampling**: A block bootstrap
resamples contiguous segments of the paired-difference sequence. Pairing keeps
each baseline and candidate case together, while blocks preserve local
dependence under the method's assumptions [@Kunsch1989BlockBootstrap].

Consider a future, fully retained matched run that defines improvement as
baseline latency minus candidate latency, so a positive value means the
candidate is faster. Suppose its point estimate were 0.3\ ms and its 95 percent
interval ran from -0.1\ ms to 0.7\ ms. These are invented teaching values, not
measurements reported by this book or calculations from the constructed
Lighthouse fixture. If the future run retained matched frame sequences and used a
declared paired block-resampling procedure, the interval would span both a
small regression and a larger improvement. Because it includes zero, that
hypothetical comparison would leave the tail-latency question unresolved even
though the point estimate is favorable.

A decision margin adds a second test. If the study requires an improvement of
at least $m$, the comparison must resolve the result relative to $m$, not
merely relative to zero. A difference inside known measurement resolution or
uncertainty remains unresolved. Calling it a tie may be appropriate under a
predeclared rule, but calling it an improvement is not.

### Controlling Confounding and Selection

A matched comparison can still support the wrong explanation. Confounding
exists when another changed factor could account for the result. Stable
versions, ablations, matched contrasts, and sensitivity studies help separate
the intended change from plausible alternatives.

Selection introduces another problem. If a search evaluates many noisy
candidates and reports only the best, the selected value retains some of the
luck that made it win. Repeating the same search data does not remove that
bias [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. This book recommends measuring the
chosen candidate again on fresh seeds, workloads, or cases that did not select
it. The fresh evaluation asks whether the margin survives after the search has
stopped choosing the winner.

Even a carefully matched comparison supports nothing beyond the properties
its checks can observe. The next question is therefore not only whether the
candidate and comparator were treated alike, but whether the selected checks
bear on the claim being made.

## Qualifying Proxies and Testing Explanations {#sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration}

### Qualifying a Proxy for the Decision

An architecture proxy is useful because it is cheaper or earlier than the
quantity that ultimately matters. Estimated instructions per cycle (IPC),
analytical energy, wirelength, congestion, utilization, and cycle counts can
all help order candidates. They remain partial measurements. The danger grows
when an optimizer searches directly against them, because the search is
rewarded for finding every region where the proxy and the intended result part
company.

This is Goodhart's problem in architecture form. A measure that once tracked a
goal can stop tracking it after it becomes the optimization target
[@Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement; @Strathern1997Goodhart]. AI is not unique in
this behavior. It changes the scale and persistence of the search for
loopholes.

Observed qualification cases and held-out agreement answer separate questions
(@fig-trust-calibration). The conceptual schematic uses normalized quantities
rather than measured data. Three green bands mark distinct strata where the
proxy and stronger reference were both observed, while the dashed white band
marks an unsampled gap inside the left-hand range. Finite cases directly
establish only the sampled points or strata in named workload, candidate, tool,
and condition dimensions. Neither the curves nor the spaces between observed
strata qualify unsampled cases or dimensions.

Here, *proxy qualification* is the umbrella term. Numerical calibration refers
only to a declared mapping between proxy outputs and stronger reference
outcomes. It is not confidence calibration, which asks whether stated
probabilities or intervals match observed frequencies and is treated as a
system-evaluation question in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. Observed
qualification coverage records the sampled dimensions, strata or cases, and
gaps. Held-out error, ranking stability, uncertainty, and fitness for the
architecture decision remain separate tests.

![**Discrete qualification cases leave visible gaps**: The conceptual,
normalized curves show paired proxy and stronger-reference observations in
three sampled strata, an unsampled gap between them, and possible divergence as
search continues beyond those strata. A real study must record the dimensions,
sampled cases or strata, gaps, and held-out agreement; these curves are not
measured data.](images/F9-trust-calibration){#fig-trust-calibration width="100%"
fig-alt="Conceptual normalized plot with three separate green qualification
strata in the left-hand range. Paired proxy and stronger-reference markers
appear in each stratum, while a dashed white band marks an unsampled gap between
the first two. The curves may diverge as search continues into an unqualified
right-hand range; no plotted curve is measured data."}

The three green bands and paired markers show where both the proxy and stronger
reference were observed. The dashed band between the first two remains
unqualified even though both smooth curves pass through it. Held-out
comparisons must still show whether error and candidate ordering are adequate
for the decision at the sampled strata. Movement into the internal gap or
beyond the sampled strata requires additional justification or new reference
checks. The widening separation on the right illustrates why the available
evidence does not support treating a higher proxy score as a stronger result
without those checks.

Representative held-out samples can support more than claims about the exact
sampled points. When the target population, sampling design, assumptions, and
uncertainty are declared, they can support a bounded population-level claim
[@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. That statistical inference does not qualify
arbitrary unobserved workload,
candidate, tool, or condition regions outside the population and sampling
design.

Numerical calibration and ranking fidelity answer different questions. A
numerically calibrated scalar mapping relates proxy outputs to reference
outcomes under a declared procedure, while a predictive interval adds a stated
uncertainty model [@ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate]. Ranking fidelity asks
whether candidate ordering survives the stronger check. Low average error can
coexist with the wrong ordering near the decision boundary, while a useful
ordering can coexist with biased absolute values. Qualification therefore
reports the relationship needed by the decision and tests its error or
instability against the declared margin.

Six problems should be tested separately (@tbl-proxy-diagnostics).

| **Concern** | **Diagnostic check** | **What an adverse result means** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Proxy mismatch** | Compare the proxy with a more decision-relevant measurement on matched cases. | The available evidence does not support carrying the proxy result to the stronger claim. |
| **Observed qualification coverage** | Record the workload, candidate, tool, and condition dimensions; place matched cases across sampled strata; and identify gaps the search may enter. | The available evidence does not qualify a reported candidate outside sampled cases or inside an unqualified gap. |
| **Held-out agreement** | Measure error, ranking stability, and uncertainty against the decision margin on cases not used to fit or tune the proxy. | The available evidence does not support reliable candidate ordering for the declared use, even at observed qualification cases. |
| **Confounding** | Hold versions and budgets fixed, use matched contrasts, and test plausible alternative causes. | The difference does not identify the proposed cause. |
| **Variability** | Repeat stochastic flows or sampled workloads and report dispersion or ranking stability. | The point estimate may not resolve the declared margin. |
| **Selection bias** | Re-evaluate the selected candidate on fresh cases not used to choose it. | The apparent margin may contain the luck that made the candidate win. |

: **Each weakness requires a different diagnostic**: A second run cannot repair
a missing property, and a stronger tool cannot repair an unmatched comparator.
{#tbl-proxy-diagnostics tbl-colwidths="[18,43,39]"}

The first three rows test whether the proxy observes the relevant property,
which sampled points or strata have matched qualification cases, where gaps
remain, and whether held-out cases support the ordering needed for the decision.
The next three separate alternative causes, run-to-run variation, and the
favorable noise retained when a search selects its winner. The final column
states which inference an adverse result removes. One failed diagnostic does
not make the other diagnoses or their repairs interchangeable.

Robustness checks stress the current claim envelope rather than silently
widening it. Workload phases, seeds, nearby candidates, tool or model
alternatives, and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners can expose a
ranking or margin that depends on one favorable case. Sensitivity to those
declared factors narrows, contradicts, or supports the current result. A changed
objective or specification first reopens the proxy relationships that depend on
it. If the change alters what success means for the target decision, the old
qualification no longer answers the same question and must not be presented as
a robustness result.

The public debate over learned macro placement illustrates why qualification and
matched comparison matter. Proxy metrics such as wirelength and congestion do
not automatically settle post-route power, performance, and area, and public
assessments have differed in tool flow, baseline strength, pretraining, and
available design data [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement;
@GoldieEtAl2024AlphaChipAddendum; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment;
@GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed]. The durable lesson is not a verdict on one
placement method. It is that a proxy comparison cannot silently inherit strength
from a stronger result obtained under unmatched conditions.

Qualified measurements still do not choose among performance, power, and area.
Each quantity retains its unit and uncertainty, and hard constraints remain
separate. Any aggregate ranking must declare its normalization, weights, or
dominance rule. If two candidates remain nondominated, the feedback exposes an
architecture tradeoff rather than manufacturing a winner
[@Deb2001MultiObjective].

A simulator can also be the exploited reference. In Gupta et al.'s
architecture-agent study, a ChampSim assertion against last-level-cache write
bypass was eliminated by the optimized build, so that configuration did not
enforce the intended correctness constraint [@GuptaEtAl2026ArchAgent].
Qualifying a proxy against that run would reproduce the blind spot. The reference check
must itself retain the property, configuration, and coverage used to justify
it.

### Separating the Outcome From the Mechanism

An outcome says what changed. A mechanism says why. They require different
comparisons and can reach different statuses.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="A lower miss count is not the architecture result"}
For a future Lighthouse cache run, the outcome question would concern
99th-percentile frame time. The mechanism question would ask whether added
capacity reduces capacity misses and whether that reduction explains a
tail-latency change. Suppose a fully retained matched run reported a 12 percent
miss reduction and the hypothetical frame-time interval above. The percentage
is also an invented teaching value, not a measurement reported by this book. If
qualified under the stated conditions, the lower miss count would support only
an intermediate effect within the cache model. It would not prove the mechanism
or the architecture outcome, and an interval crossing zero would leave the
frame-time comparison unresolved.
:::

The reverse can also occur. A candidate may improve the measured outcome while
the proposed explanation fails. The improvement can remain a valid observation
if the comparison is sound, but an unresolved or contradicted mechanism should
not guide the next change. A plausible model explanation is a hypothesis, not
a substitute for a contrast.

Useful mechanism checks include matched workload contrasts, ablations,
counterfactual configurations, traces of the affected events, and sensitivity
around the changed parameter. They should be declared before the result when
possible. Otherwise, an explanation can be fitted to any outcome after the
fact. A contrast identifies a cause only when the intervention is well defined
and plausible alternative paths are ruled out by the design or bounded by
explicit identification assumptions [@Pearl2009Causality]. The resulting
judgments must remain separate even when they come from the same study
(@tbl-outcome-mechanism).

| **Question** | **Possible status** | **Hypothetical Lighthouse illustration** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Did the requested quantity change in the declared direction?** | Supported, contradicted, or unresolved within the stated comparison. | If the invented interval included zero, tail frame-time improvement would remain unresolved. |
| **Did the proposed intermediate effect occur?** | Supported, contradicted, unresolved, or not tested. | If a qualified future run found capacity misses 12 percent lower, that result would support a bounded intermediate effect. |
| **Did that intermediate effect cause the outcome?** | Supported only by a distinguishing intervention or contrast under stated identification assumptions; otherwise unresolved. | Even then, the causal link between fewer misses and tail latency would remain unresolved without a distinguishing check. |
| **What did the check not observe?** | Explicit nonclaims. | Such a cache-local result would not establish thermal behavior, voltage-droop behavior, functional correctness, security, or system-level extended-reality (XR) quality. |

: **Outcome and mechanism remain separate results**: A supported intermediate
effect cannot fill an unresolved architecture comparison.
{#tbl-outcome-mechanism tbl-colwidths="[26,30,44]"}

The important pattern is asymmetric support. An outcome and an intermediate
effect may resolve while the proposed cause remains open, and a supported cause
cannot widen the set of properties the check observed. For architecture work,
that means a local cache result can guide the next cache experiment without
becoming a claim about thermal, electrical, functional, security, or system
behavior.

This separation makes negative results useful. A contradicted mechanism can
improve the architecture model even when the candidate result is favorable. A
resolved regression can rule out a design direction. An unresolved comparison
can reveal that the observation budget or measurement plan was too weak. None
of those outcomes is a failed study if the record keeps them distinct.

Both Lighthouse candidates remain open for different reasons. The 4\ MiB entry
depicts no simulator request but supplies no parser or dispatch evidence for a
verified no-dispatch action. The 3\ MiB entries distinguish a stale-state setup
failure from later returns that lack the values, artifacts, state identity, and
lineage needed for qualification. Neither sequence can establish physical
limits, miss behavior, tail latency, or a mechanism. Those unresolved
requirements determine which checks must be matched to the claims next.

## Matching Checks to Claims {#sec-independent-checks-and-correlated-errors}

A supported difference is not the same as adequate requirement coverage. This
section asks whether each material architecture requirement has a suitable
check path and whether those paths cover the claim.

This chapter keeps structured assurance information in the cumulative study
record rather than reducing a result to one confidence score. Assurance-case practice motivates the
claim-specific structure [@Kelly2004GSN], but the chapter does not import a
second project process. The record names the property and scope, check
coverage and possible error direction, shared assumptions, formal proof status
where applicable, empirical and model uncertainty, the basis for any
independence claim, explicit nonclaims, and the consequence of being wrong.
These fields cannot be averaged into one number. Increasing confidence means
reducing or bounding relevant failure paths for a named claim. Agreement
between checks that share the same blind spot does not reduce the risk
contributed by that shared blind spot. A proved property can coexist with
uncertain performance, incomplete workload coverage, and an untested security
claim.

Some architecture results depend on confidential workloads, design data, or
tool flows. They can support an internal conclusion when an authorized reviewer
can inspect the complete record and challenge its method, scope, uncertainty,
and limits. A public claim must remain within what public material or an audit
by a reviewer with access to the protected record can establish.
Confidentiality does not turn a production report into an independently
replayable comparison.

### Connecting Requirements to Checks

Requirement satisfaction does not mean that all performed checks passed. Each
declared material requirement or hard constraint must map to a named artifact
and conditions, an acceptance criterion, a check path suited to the property,
empirical uncertainty or formal status, shared assumptions, and the uncovered
remainder. A missing or unqualified mapping leaves that requirement unresolved,
even when every other performed check passes. Passing the mapped checks does
not establish that the requirement set is complete.

A confidence interval can support a statistical performance or reliability
requirement when the target population, sampling assumptions, risk criterion,
and decision margin are declared. Some yield and manufacturing requirements are
also statistical and must retain their population and variation model. A hard
timing, power, or design-rule acceptance limit instead requires the project's
designated signoff method to resolve the acceptance rule under named modes,
corners, modeled variation, and uncertainty. A favorable point estimate is not
a hard-limit pass. If the designated analysis cannot establish the acceptable
side of the limit under those conditions, the requirement remains unresolved.

The unexecuted Lighthouse cache study makes the mappings concrete without
inventing a candidate result.

- **Request, artifact, and interface legality:** Schema, type, translation, and
  interface checks must bind the exact request and artifacts to their tool and
  parser versions. The constructed record lacks translated inputs and parser
  evidence, so this mapping is unqualified.
- **SRAM area and access-time thresholds:** The operational threshold check
  needs a complete, schema-valid SRAM artifact with units, model and PVT
  conditions, parser status, and a qualified bound or error direction. The
  constructed values are illustrative and the retained evidence is
  insufficient, so these thresholds remain unqualified.
- **99th-percentile frame time:** A matched performance comparison needs
  baseline and candidate frame records, the declared statistic, workload and
  simulator conditions, and uncertainty relative to the decision margin. The
  constructed record lacks the matched frames, values, state identities, and
  uncertainty needed for that comparison, so the requirement is unqualified.
- **Subsystem 3\ W power target:** A power check needs a qualified subsystem
  power result under the declared workload, software, model, and operating
  conditions, with uncertainty or a justified bound relative to 3\ W. The
  constructed power returns lack the required artifacts and conditions, so the
  target is unqualified.
- **Functional correctness, security, and system-level XR quality:** These
  requirements need property-specific functional checks, security tests or
  analyses, and system-level evaluation. The constructed SRAM and cycle-level
  branches do not cover them, so they remain uncovered.

The first four mappings are neither passes nor failures. Their evidence is
unqualified. The final requirements are uncovered, and all candidate choices
remain open.

### What Different Checks Establish

A valid measurement may still address the wrong property. Syntax checks,
functional simulation, model checking, performance simulation, synthesis,
timing analysis, power analysis, and post-silicon characterization answer
different questions. Their strength is not a single ordering from weak to
strong. A parser can conclusively reject an illegal request while an expensive
timing run says nothing about functional correctness. Representative check
boundaries make that mismatch explicit without implying a universal ordering
(@tbl-check-scope).

| **Check class** | **What it can support within stated conditions** | **What it does not establish by itself** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Syntax and interface** | Legal encoding, type, schema, instruction set architecture (ISA), application binary interface (ABI), or protocol form. | Functional behavior, performance, physical feasibility, or system intent. |
| **Functional simulation and testing** | Behavior for exercised stimuli and observed properties. | Unexercised behaviors, physical timing, power, or unspecified security properties. |
| **Formal property and equivalence checks** | A stated property over a modeled transition system, or a stated relation between two artifacts. | Whether the property captures intent, whether assumptions match deployment, or unrelated properties. |
| **Architecture performance and power models** | Quantities represented by the model for the declared workload and configuration. | Effects the abstraction omits or behavior outside its validated region. |
| **Implementation and physical analysis** | Timing, area, power, integrity, or rule results for the modeled design, constraints, modes, and corners. | Missing constraints, unmodeled conditions, functional intent, or manufactured variation outside the analysis. |
| **Post-silicon and operational measurement** | Behavior of sampled parts and systems under measured conditions. | Every manufactured part, workload, environment, lifetime condition, or unmeasured property. |

: **A check is decisive only for the property it observes**: More cost or later
placement in a flow does not widen that property.
{#tbl-check-scope tbl-colwidths="[22,39,39]"}

The checks are complementary rather than a hierarchy from weak to strong. A later
or more expensive check can settle one implementation property while leaving
functional intent, security, or an earlier interface obligation untouched.
Architecture claims therefore need coverage across the material properties,
not merely progress to the most expensive available tool stage.

The property a check observes is only half of the measurement plan. The
intended use of its result also matters. A mistaken local ranking can waste
evaluation budget and change which candidates the search examines. A mistaken
result used to revise a shared artifact or interface can propagate across
hardware, software, verification, and integration work. The feedback plan
should therefore grow with the cost of being wrong and the difficulty of
reversing the result's technical consequences
(@tbl-feedback-by-consequence).

| **Intended use of the result** | **Consequence if the result is wrong** | **Feedback plan should include** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Choose the next local evaluation** | A candidate is explored unnecessarily, a promising one is deferred, or scarce tool time is spent on the wrong question. | Candidate identity, a matched comparator, known proxy limits, and enough precision to choose the next check. |
| **Revise a shared implementation or interface** | Hardware, software, verification, or integration work may inherit the error. | Relevant regression and compatibility checks, explicit shared assumptions, and a different check path for critical properties where practical. |
| **Support a high-consequence technical conclusion** | The error may survive into later work where it is expensive to find or reverse. | Checks covering each material claim, uncertainty relative to the decision margin, a sufficiently different path where shared failure matters, and explicit unmeasured properties. |

: **The feedback plan follows consequence and reversibility**: More costly
checks are not automatically more informative; the plan must cover the claims
and failure modes that matter for the result's intended use. This technical
assessment does not authorize the resulting action.
{#tbl-feedback-by-consequence tbl-colwidths="[27,32,41]"}

The pattern is that evidence burden follows propagation and reversibility. A
wrong local choice may waste tool time; a wrong shared-interface revision can
spread through hardware, software, verification, and integration; a wrong
high-consequence conclusion can survive into expensive work. The feedback plan
must grow with that exposure, but technical support still does not authorize
the resulting action.

### Describing the Check and Its Limits

Three questions that many tool reports omit make a check reviewable.

**Coverage.** Which failures can the check observe, and which relevant failures
leave no signal?

**Possible error direction.** Under the declared model and conditions, is the
result known to be conservative, optimistic, or neither? This must be
established for the particular flow. A pre-route estimate is not always
optimistic, and a deterministic computation is not automatically a safe
bound.

Static timing analysis illustrates why the error direction is conditional.
Cadence documents concurrent multi-mode, multi-corner analysis and statistical
on-chip variation analysis in Tempus [@Cadence2021Tempus]. The architecture
lesson is broader than those product capabilities. A result may be deliberately
pessimistic, but that claim applies only to the declared timing mode, process,
voltage, and temperature corner, derates, constraints, and modeled effects. A
pass or failure is meaningful within those conditions, not as a universal
bound. Sampled simulation has a different shape. A failing trace rejects the
exercised behavior, but a passing sample says nothing about unexercised stimuli
or properties absent from the testbench.

**Shared assumptions.** Which specifications, models, data, workloads,
constraints, code, and tool paths are shared with the producer or with another
check? A different program name or model instance does not create
independence.

Agreement adds information only when the second path changes the relevant
failure source (@fig-independent-checks). The alternative need not claim
perfect independence. It must observe the disputed property through a
sufficiently different path to reduce a known shared failure.

![**A second check adds information only when it changes the relevant failure
path**: A critic using the same assumptions can repeat the producer's omission.
A claim-specific check based on a sufficiently different model or measurement
path can reduce that correlation, but its remaining shared inputs and blind
spots must still be recorded.](images/ch7_independent_checks){#fig-independent-checks
width="92%" fig-alt="Two-column diagram. A producer and
critic sharing the same assumptions lead to correlated agreement. A producer
and a claim-specific check with a different measurement path lead to a
bounded challenge, with remaining shared assumptions explicitly retained."}

In the left path, the candidate producer and critic use the same specification
and model, so agreement remains correlated. In the right path, a claim-specific
check observes the disputed property differently and produces a bounded
challenge. The note beneath both
paths sets the limit. Some assumptions and inputs may remain shared, so a
different path can reduce correlation without proving independence.

Two uses of a second path should not be conflated. Independent qualification
of the same record challenges extraction, arithmetic, or bookkeeping. A
separate parser can recover a value from the raw report, and an independent
calculation can check its aggregation. Both may still inherit the original
tool's model, workload, and constraints. They strengthen confidence in what
that tool returned without testing whether the tool observed the right
physical property.

A materially different observation path challenges more of the claim. Another
simulator with different models, an RTL property check, a physical-design
measurement, or a direct hardware observation may expose an error that record
requalification cannot. It also has shared assumptions that must be named.
The useful question is not whether the second path deserves the label
*independent*. It is which failure source changes and which one remains shared.

Separate teams can fail together on the same hard inputs. Knight and Leveson
found correlated failures among independently developed program versions,
showing that separate implementation does not guarantee independent error
[@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. The same warning applies to a generator and
critic that share a foundation model, training data, objective, or
specification. Agreement can be useful corroboration without being an
independent check.

The missing-property case is different. Spectre and Meltdown exploited
microarchitectural side effects that ordinary functional correctness does not
constrain [@LippEtAl2018Meltdown; @KocherEtAl2019Spectre]. More functional
tests of ordinary program outputs would not settle confidentiality. Tests
designed around leakage can bear on the security claim, while an ordinary
performance suite cannot.

Checks also need checks. Mutation testing injects faults and reports which ones
a suite detects [@DeMilloLiptonSayward1978Hints]. A mutation score says
something only about the injected fault model, and equivalent or unobservable
mutants need careful handling. For AI-authored assertions and testbenches, the
useful fault set should resemble errors the generator actually makes rather
than only traditional hand-written mistakes.

A check can be valid for the property it observes and still be only a proxy
for the architecture objective. Functional simulation may establish agreement
for tested inputs without settling performance, while a cycle estimate may
rank candidates without establishing timing closure. The remaining question
is how far the cheaper observation can carry the stronger claim.

A technical conclusion can be supported only when the identified material
requirements are mapped, the supporting artifacts and results are qualified,
uncertainty is resolved relative to the acceptance margins, and a sufficiently
different failure path is used where the consequence warrants it. Completeness
of the requirement set remains unresolved, and residual unknowns and explicit
nonclaims remain part of the conclusion. This technical support does not
authorize architecture commitment. It establishes what feedback may justify as
the next technical action.

## Routing the Next Technical Action

Once a qualified result supports, contradicts, or leaves unresolved a named
claim, feedback turns that status into direction for the work. It identifies
the object that needs attention and the next technical action. The signal does
not prescribe its own update, and the technical action does not by itself
authorize an architecture commitment.

An incomplete or invalid execution record routes directly to the environment
before verification or feedback. For statuses established later, feedback
directs attention to the object implicated by the qualified or verified result
(@tbl-feedback-destinations).

| **Established status** | **Object needing attention** | **Resulting move** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The execution record is incomplete or invalid. | Tool-connected environment | Repair extraction, state, lineage, or invocation before interpreting the candidate. |
| The represented state or dependency is wrong. | Design representation | Correct the represented problem and invalidate results that used the wrong state. |
| A qualified architecture effect is observed. | Project record; design owner if revision is supported | Record the bounded result and revise the design only when the result supports that move. |
| A proxy leaves its support or shows systematic error. | Approach choice or qualification study | Recalibrate, narrow, replace, or stop using the proxy. Do not create training labels automatically. |
| Human review exposes a missing constraint or assumption. | Study formulation or representation | Record the rationale and revise the object that omitted the requirement. |
| The outcome is resolved but its proposed mechanism is not. | Study formulation | Preserve the result and add a distinguishing contrast before using the explanation to guide another change. |
| The comparison remains unresolved. | Measurement plan or study formulation | Improve the contrast, precision target, observation budget, or stopping rule. |
| A reviewed formal counterexample is realizable under the intended conditions. | Design or represented problem | Preserve the trace and revise the design or requirement that it contradicts. If setup, property, or assumptions are wrong, repair those first. |
| A formal proof establishes the declared property. | Project record | Record the scoped result and discharge only the claim that the property, model, assumptions, and proof mode cover. |
| A formal result is bounded-only or inconclusive. | Proof or measurement plan | Revise the abstraction, assumptions, bound, method, or resource budget. Do not relabel the result as a pass. |
| A matched comparison resolves that any difference is smaller than the declared decision margin. | Project record | Preserve the result without forcing a design or model update. |
| A qualified failed check is accepted as a bounded exception. | Project record and responsible owner | Preserve the failed status, waiver scope, rationale, compensating control, residual risk, expiration, and reopening condition. |

: **Established status determines the next technical move**: Execution failure
routes directly to the environment before verification or feedback. Qualified
or verified results then let feedback direct repair, recording, revision,
requalification, or no change at the relevant object.
{#tbl-feedback-destinations tbl-colwidths="[32,25,43]"}

The table has one recurring pattern. A qualified status routes attention to the
object that can repair or use it, while unsupported inferences remain open.
Some results justify no design change at all. A difference below the declared
margin updates the project record, a proof discharges only its stated property,
and a waiver preserves a failure as a scoped exception. No route turns a tool
failure or unresolved comparison into a training label automatically.

::: {.callout-field-note title="An illustrative timing return produces a bounded action"}
**The expectation.** A qualified timing return should support a bounded claim
and eligible repair, not a conclusion about the whole pipeline.

**In practice.** This example is illustrative, not empirical project evidence.
For mapped netlist `CPU-NL-17`, constraint set `CPU-SDC-17`, and corner
`SS_0P72V_125C`, the return for path `EX-MEM-P17` reports
$-0.04\,\mathrm{ns}$ setup slack from `U_EX/alu_sum_reg[17]/Q` to
`U_MEM/addr_reg[17]/D`. Complete tool status,
constrained endpoints, clock model, derates, and report lineage qualify the
value for that named setup check. The bounded claim is that this path violates
its zero-slack setup requirement under the declared conditions. It says nothing
about hold timing, function, power, another corner, or global feasibility. That
claim makes moving a pipeline boundary or reducing logic depth eligible,
followed by logical equivalence, functional regression, and setup-and-hold
reruns for every affected mode and corner.

**The lesson.** Retain the failing path and conditions with the repair
rationale. Reopen the result whenever the netlist, constraint set, clock model,
derates, or affected path endpoints change.
:::

A qualified status makes a technical action eligible; it does not schedule the
next attempt. An invalid execution permits environment repair, a qualified
hard-constraint violation permits candidate rejection or revision, and an
unresolved comparison permits a better measurement or contrast. A retry is
eligible only when a linked attempt could resolve the pending decision within
the remaining budget. @sec-running-the-loop owns how eligible actions are
scheduled, repeated, budgeted, and stopped. This chapter establishes what the
signal can justify. Defects that block validity or required correctness still
take precedence over optional performance refinement.

When two feedback sources appear to conflict, first align the candidate,
property, conditions, versions, and aggregation. The signals may concern
different scopes rather than contradict one claim. If they still conflict,
inspect shared assumptions and known error directions, then choose a
distinguishing check targeted at the disputed property. When neither result
can be shown to supersede the other, preserve both as unresolved. Do not
average incompatible signals or select a source by prestige.

A reviewer's observation is feedback. Approval is a separate, authorized
project action. Neither makes an unsupported result valid. Approval may accept
bounded residual risk, but it cannot supply a missing measurement or check.
Final architecture commitment remains separate and belongs to
@sec-what-architect-owns.

Some failed checks can remain open under a bounded waiver accepted by an
authorized owner. The waiver does not turn the failed result into a pass. It
retains the failed check, rationale, exact scope, responsible owner,
compensating check or control, residual risk, expiration or review condition,
and reopening trigger. Waiver support in a physical-verification flow can
preserve waived design-rule violations and their associated text. Siemens
documents this behavior for Calibre Auto-Waivers, which applies the records
across later design rule checking (DRC) runs
[@SiemensCalibreAutoWaivers]. The technical record belongs here. Authority to
accept the residual risk belongs to
@sec-what-architect-owns.

## Learning From Qualified Feedback

Learning here means a justified change to what the work does or retains, not an
automatic model update. Within the current run, a qualified SRAM access-time
violation can make the predeclared no-dispatch action eligible for that cache
candidate. An architect or method may then evaluate a smaller cache, revise the
memory organization, or end that branch through the run controls in
@sec-running-the-loop.
Across the current project, an interface counterexample that has been reviewed
and shown realizable under the intended conditions can add a retained protocol
constraint and regression test, correct the represented state, withdraw
qualification from an affected component, and record which interface change
would reopen earlier results. For later work, the qualified range, held-out
checks, and failed cases for a cache proxy can be preserved as scoped artifacts
and lessons. Another project may reuse them, but it must re-establish the
conclusions under the transfer conditions described in
@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack.

Project learning and model learning are different. A design constraint,
contradicted comparison, supported intermediate effect, or supported mechanism
can update project state without becoming training data. A model update needs a
named target, usable labels, scope, and acceptance test. Tool failures,
unmatched results, and unresolved comparisons should not become simple pass or
fail labels.

The cumulative study record indexes mechanisms architects already use. These
include verification plans, requirements traceability, regression and coverage
databases, signoff reports, waiver records, and change-impact tracking. The
record links them to the claims and decisions they support; it does not replace
them with a parallel workflow or another bureaucracy.

### Updating a Learned Component

An updated model or proxy is a new component version within the design system
[@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden]. In architecture work, that version change can
invalidate candidate rankings, proxy scope, and cached search decisions that
depended on the previous component. Architecture search also chooses which
candidates receive expensive labels, so the labeled outcomes are
policy-selected and the missing outcomes are not random. Active learning studies
how a method chooses which example to label next [@Settles2009ActiveLearning];
@sec-data-representations-world-models introduced the corresponding
selective-acquisition problem for architecture data. Learning only from returned
labels can reinforce the regions the current search already favors and preserve
its blind spots.

Before the component reenters the design process, the project records the
update data, the acquisition policy, and the retained selection decisions,
including candidates that did not receive labels. It tests failure-relevant
cases and previously qualified cases or strata that were not used for the
update, repeats the decision-relevant error, ranking, or proxy-qualification
checks, and looks for regressions. This book recommends randomized or stratified
audit evaluations that probe cases outside the policy's choices where
practical.

When acceptance results steer subsequent updates, repeated use turns those
cases into development data, just as adaptive reuse can overfit a holdout set
[@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout]. The project must therefore keep acceptance cases
untouched or refresh them. This book recommends keeping the updated component
outside the active process until it passes a shadow evaluation that does not
steer candidate selection, or a sufficiently independent acceptance path. It
then reenters with revised qualification scope and reopening conditions rather
than inheriting the previous version's scope. Passing these checks qualifies the
new component version for its declared use. It does not inherit the architecture
conclusions supported by the old version.

### Reopening and Requalifying

Reopening marks the conditions under which an old interpretation must be
requalified. A changed workload, software image, model, tool, operating
condition, candidate revision, artifact, interface, requirement, proxy
calibration result, or contrary observation can reopen dependent claims without
predetermining the next revision. The project identifies which binding or
relationship may no longer hold. It does not silently invalidate unrelated
results.

Distribution shift occurs when the data-generating conditions encountered in
use differ from those represented during development or qualification
[@QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift]. In architecture work, the change can be
a new workload mix, movement into a different candidate region, or a new
distribution of process, voltage, and temperature conditions. This chapter uses
*drift signal* for an observed change over time in those conditions or in the
proxy's residuals, interval coverage, or ranking stability. Such a signal does
not identify its cause, and it does not by itself authorize retraining.

Many changes remain within the same project and current target decision. A
tightened timing constraint may reopen only the requirement comparison and
margin that used the old limit; a qualified timing measurement can remain intact
when its artifact and conditions have not changed. A revised reset or interface
version may reopen the functional, formal, and integration checks that consumed
it while leaving unrelated measurements intact. The project traces each claim
and check to the workload, tool or model, artifact, condition, interface, and
requirement it depends on. It reruns the minimum adequate affected checks and
keeps an unaffected claim only with a recorded rationale.

A candidate, configuration, tool, or operating-condition mismatch can make an
affected execution record stale and require lineage repair or a rerun of the
same check. Changed workload populations, phase coverage, or movement among
candidate cases can require new sampling and repeated qualification.
Deteriorating proxy-reference residuals, interval coverage, or ranking stability
can require narrowing,
recalibrating, replacing, or stopping the proxy. Relearning is one possible
response only when the proxy is a learned component and an independent
acceptance test exists.

The boundary changes when the objective's meaning, legal action space, artifact
boundary, or acceptance semantics change enough to define a new target
decision. Determining what prior results carry into that target is a transfer
problem rather than selective requalification within the current decision
(@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack). Until that boundary is crossed, the project
preserves each old result and its scope, names the affected dependencies and
minimum adequate checks, and lets the new evidence determine the update.

## Open Research Questions

**Qualifying measurements and checks.**

- **How can an unfamiliar tool return from an AI-assisted design loop be
  qualified before it influences a design?** A system must recover what
  produced the value, which artifact and property it concerns, its unit and
  conditions, and what the producing tool could not observe. One experiment
  could perturb report schemas, warnings, units, and versions while holding
  tool semantics fixed, then measure semantic recovery, safe rejection, and
  downstream decision errors against expert-labeled records.

- **How can correlated failure be measured across apparently independent
  checks in an AI-assisted design loop?** Different tools, models, reviewers,
  and modalities may still share a specification error, workload blind spot,
  library, or training source. One experiment could seed a shared requirement
  or workload omission across otherwise distinct check paths, then measure
  false corroboration and whether assumption tracing or a different observation
  path exposes it.

**Strengthening verification.**

- **How can AI-authored tests and properties be checked for semantic omissions
  or insufficient strength?** Generated verification collateral may be
  syntactically valid and nonvacuous while omitting required protocol, timing,
  reset, security, ordering, exclusivity, progress, or environmental behavior.
  One experiment could remove named requirements or inject known protocol,
  reset, and security faults, then compare generated collateral with expert
  verification plans on detection, vacuity, requirement coverage, and false
  assurance.

**Learning and requalifying feedback.**

- **How can an AI-assisted architecture system learn from policy-selected,
  censored, delayed, and expensive outcomes without amplifying blind spots or
  inheriting unsupported scope?** Architecture search determines which
  candidates receive labels, so observed outcomes may preserve the current
  policy's blind spots. One experiment could send a randomized audit subset of
  logged candidates to stronger checks, then compare update methods on fresh
  failure-region coverage, decision quality, label delay, and verification
  cost.

- **How can an AI-assisted design system select the minimum adequate checks to
  rerun after a within-study change?** Dependencies between claims and checks
  are often incomplete, while unnecessary reruns consume scarce tool time. A
  versioned set of changes with known affected requirements and artifacts could
  compare impact-analysis methods on missed invalidations, unnecessary reruns,
  and the cost required to regain supported status.

## Conclusion {#sec-trust-boundary-conclusion}

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Useful feedback carries its source, scope, and limits"}
Feedback can guide learning only when the record names its producer, target,
meaning, timing, scope, and quality limits. Dense proxy feedback can guide local
revision inside its validated range. Less frequent feedback can test
decision-relevant properties the proxy omits. Neither supports an update beyond
what it actually observed.
:::

An architect can turn a returned signal into a bounded architecture result only
after establishing execution and artifact validity, qualifying the relevant
measurement or formal status, and matching the check to the claim. That status
controls the eligible technical action. Learning retains the result, its
reason, its limits, and the condition that would reopen it.

The unresolved question is orchestration. A multi-step study must schedule and
stop eligible actions without losing state, cost, lineage, or their rationale.
@sec-running-the-loop takes up that problem.
